---
title: "Multi-Omics and Multimodal Integration"
---

A modern experiment rarely observes one modality. The same cell or sample can be
measured by transcriptome, surface protein, chromatin accessibility, spatial
location, and histology, and each view carries information the others miss. The
integration problem is to build a representation that is *shared* enough to
compare and transfer across modalities, yet *specific* enough to preserve what
each modality uniquely contributes. This chapter covers fusion strategies,
shared-latent-space models, contrastive alignment, cross-modal translation,
missing-modality handling, and spatial transcriptomics as a case study.

::: {.callout-note}
## Definition
**Multimodal integration** learns a joint representation of two or more data
modalities measured on the same units (cells, spots, or samples). A **shared
latent space** contains factors that explain variation common to all modalities;
**modality-specific** factors explain variation unique to one view. A good
integration preserves both.
:::

# The Integration Problem: Shared and Modality-Specific Factors

Write each unit $i$ as a set of observations
$\{\mathbf{x}_i^{(1)},\dots,\mathbf{x}_i^{(M)}\}$ over $M$ modalities, with
$\mathbf{x}_i^{(m)}\in\mathcal{X}_m$ the measurement of modality $m$. A generative
view posits a shared latent vector
$\mathbf{z}_i^{\mathrm{sh}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{sh}}}$, per-modality latent
vectors $\mathbf{z}_i^{(m)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_m}$, and a covariate vector
$\mathbf{c}_i$ collecting technical variables such as library size and batch:
$$
\mathbf{x}_i^{(m)}
\;\sim\; p_{\theta_m}\!\left(\,\cdot \mid \mathbf{z}_i^{\mathrm{sh}},\, \mathbf{z}_i^{(m)},\, \mathbf{c}_i\right),
\qquad m=1,\dots,M,
$$ {#eq-ch09-factor-model}
where $\theta_m$ are the decoder parameters of modality $m$ and each
$p_{\theta_m}$ is a modality-appropriate likelihood (a count model for RNA, a
Bernoulli for binarized accessibility, and so on). The shared factor drives
cross-modal prediction and alignment; the private factors absorb modality-specific
structure. @eq-ch09-factor-model carries one substantive assumption — that the
modalities are **conditionally independent given the latents**,
$p(\mathbf{x}_i^{(1)},\dots,\mathbf{x}_i^{(M)}\mid\cdot)=\prod_m p_{\theta_m}(\mathbf{x}_i^{(m)}\mid\cdot)$
— which is what licenses a separate likelihood term per modality during inference.
This decomposition is the organizing idea behind every method in this chapter,
whether it is fit by factor analysis [@argelaguet2020mofa] or by a deep generative
model [@ashuach2023multivi; @gong2021cobolt].

::: {.callout-note}
## Definition
**Fusion strategy** describes *where* modalities are combined: **early fusion**
concatenates features before modeling, **late fusion** trains per-modality models
and combines their outputs, and **intermediate fusion** combines learned
representations inside a model, producing a shared latent space.
:::

The recurring trade-off is quantitative, not merely conceptual. Let
$I(\cdot;\cdot)$ denote mutual information and $H(\cdot\mid\cdot)$ conditional
entropy (Appendix A), and let $\mathbf{x}^{(m)}$ denote the (random) modality-$m$
profile of a unit. For two modalities the dependence decomposes as
$$
I\big(\mathbf{x}^{(1)};\mathbf{x}^{(2)}\big)
= H\big(\mathbf{x}^{(1)}\big) - H\big(\mathbf{x}^{(1)}\mid\mathbf{x}^{(2)}\big),
$$ {#eq-ch09-mi-decomp}
where $H(\mathbf{x}^{(1)}\mid\mathbf{x}^{(2)})$ is exactly the component of
modality 1 that is *unique* to it. Any representation
$\mathbf{z}=g(\mathbf{x}^{(1)})$ built from modality 1 alone satisfies, by the
data-processing inequality,
$$
I\big(\mathbf{z};\mathbf{x}^{(2)}\big)\;\le\;I\big(\mathbf{x}^{(1)};\mathbf{x}^{(2)}\big),
$$ {#eq-ch09-dpi}
so an encoder optimized only for cross-modal agreement can recover at most the
shared term of @eq-ch09-mi-decomp, and the private term
$H(\mathbf{x}^{(1)}\mid\mathbf{x}^{(2)})$ is invisible to it. The right operating
point depends on whether the downstream task needs transfer between modalities
(favor the shared term) or within-modality resolution (retain the private terms).
A useful way to make the trade-off concrete is to ask, for a candidate embedding,
three measurable questions: (i) how much of modality 2 can be predicted from the
shared space learned from modality 1 alone, measured by
$I(\mathbf{z};\mathbf{x}^{(2)})$ (alignment / transfer); (ii) how much
within-modality structure is preserved when the shared space is the only feature,
measured by $I(\mathbf{z}^{(1)};\mathbf{x}^{(1)})$ for the private representation
$\mathbf{z}^{(1)}$ (resolution / information retention); and (iii) how much
cross-modal *unique* signal is confined to a private factor, measured by
$H(\mathbf{x}^{(1)}\mid\mathbf{x}^{(2)})$ (specificity). By @eq-ch09-dpi no
single embedding maximizes all three, which is why the choice is task-dependent
rather than universal.

Different modality pairs also pose different difficulties:

| Modality pair | Example assay | Main difficulty |
|---|---|---|
| RNA + protein | CITE-seq [@stoeckius2017simultaneous] | Count models differ (NB vs. protein); shared space must reconcile scales |
| RNA + chromatin | 10x Multiome | Very different sparsity and dimensionality; binary vs. count |
| Expression + space | Spatial transcriptomics [@biancalani2021deep; @hu2021spagcn] | Reference has no coordinates; alignment is a matching problem |
| Expression + histology | Spatial imaging | Continuous image features vs. discrete counts |
| Sequence + structure | AlphaFold-era data [@jumper2021highly] | Alignment across a prediction, not an observation |

# Fusion Strategies and Shared-Latent-Space Models

## A comparison of fusion strategies

| Strategy | How it works | Strengths | Weaknesses | Representative methods |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Early fusion | Concatenate features (or normalize then concatenate) | Simple; one model | Scale/sparsity mismatch; batch-driven; cannot handle missing views | Baseline concatenation + PCA |
| Late fusion | Predict per modality, combine outputs | Modular; robust to view-specific noise | No shared representation; cannot transfer across modalities | Ensemble WNN-style label voting [@hao2021integrated] |
| Intermediate (shared-latent) | Encode each view, combine in latent space | Transferable, handles missing views, interpretable factors | Harder to train; alignment vs. privacy trade-off | MOFA+ [@argelaguet2020mofa], MultiVI [@ashuach2023multivi], Cobolt [@gong2021cobolt] |
| Contrastive alignment | Align paired embeddings with a contrastive loss | Strong cross-modal retrieval; no shared decoder needed | Needs paired data; sensitive to negatives | CLIP-style objectives [@radford2021learning] |

Early fusion is the simplest baseline and has a clear failure mode:
concatenating RNA counts with protein counts, or with a high-dimensional image
feature vector, produces a matrix whose geometry is dominated by whichever
modality has the larger scale and sparsity, and it cannot represent a unit with a
missing view. Late fusion avoids the scale mismatch but forfeits a shared space
and therefore cross-modal transfer. Intermediate and contrastive fusion are the
strategies that provide both.

## MOFA+: factor analysis across modalities

MOFA+ [@argelaguet2020mofa] is a probabilistic factor-analysis model. It
decomposes each modality's matrix into a small number of factors with
per-modality weight matrices and per-modality variance terms, learning factors
that are shared where the data support sharing and inactive where they are not.
Because it is a linear, Bayesian model, the factors are directly interpretable as
the axes along which modalities align, and missing views are handled natively
within the inference. Its limitation is the same as any linear method: nonlinear
manifold structure in a single modality is not captured.

## MultiVI: deep generative integration with missing modalities

MultiVI [@ashuach2023multivi] extends the scVI likelihood framework
[@lopez2018deep] to jointly model RNA and ATAC (chromatin accessibility). Each
modality has its own likelihood — a negative binomial for counts and a Bernoulli
for binarized accessibility — but both are decoded from a shared latent space. The
negative binomial here is the non-zero-inflated special case of the zero-inflated
negative binomial used by scVI in Chapter 8, and each model follows the likelihood
chosen by its source [@lopez2018deep; @ashuach2023multivi].
Crucially, MultiVI is trained so that a cell missing one modality still receives a
latent representation, enabling imputation and integration of partially observed
data. totalVI [@gayoso2021joint] applies the same principle to RNA plus surface
protein from CITE-seq [@stoeckius2017simultaneous].

## Cobolt: hierarchical multimodal alignment

Cobolt [@gong2021cobolt] uses a hierarchical variational autoencoder
[@kingma2014auto] that factorizes each cell into a shared latent and
modality-specific latents, then aligns the shared components across modalities.
It was developed in the context of single-nucleus RNA plus ATAC and is designed
to be robust to modality imbalance — the common case where one modality is much
larger or noisier than the other.

## Graph-based multimodal integration

Seurat's weighted-nearest-neighbor (WNN) approach [@hao2021integrated] takes a
different route: it builds a separate neighbor graph per modality, then weights
the modalities per cell by their local predictive information and combines the
graphs. This is intermediate fusion on a graph rather than in a Euclidean latent
space, and it is widely used because it is simple and does not require a
generative model.

## The shared-latent-space picture

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  X1["Modality 1: RNA counts"] --> E1["Encoder 1"]
  X2["Modality 2: protein or ATAC"] --> E2["Encoder 2"]
  E1 --> S["Shared latent z_shared"]
  E2 --> S
  E1 --> P1["Private z_1"]
  E2 --> P2["Private z_2"]
  S --> D1["Decoder 1 + likelihood"]
  S --> D2["Decoder 2 + likelihood"]
  P1 --> D1
  P2 --> D2
```

Every intermediate-fusion method can be read off this figure: modality-specific
encoders, a bottleneck that is partitioned into shared and private components,
and modality-specific decoders that force each view to be reconstructable from
the shared space. The design choices are where to enforce sharing (a loss term, a
joint factor prior, or a shared decoder) and how to weight reconstruction against
alignment.

# Contrastive Multimodal Alignment

An alternative to generative fusion is to learn two encoders whose embeddings
agree for paired observations and disagree otherwise, without ever reconstructing
inputs. Write $\mathbf{u}_i\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ and
$\mathbf{v}_i\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ for the modality-1 and modality-2 embeddings of
the $i$-th paired unit in a batch of size $B$, and let $\tau>0$ be a temperature;
$\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ is the inner product of Appendix A. The **InfoNCE**
loss [@vandenoord2018representation], also central to SimCLR [@chen2020simple],
is a $B$-way classification of which $\mathbf{v}$ pairs with a given
$\mathbf{u}$: for the $i$-th pair it pulls the positive pair
$(\mathbf{u}_i,\mathbf{v}_i)$ together and pushes the cross pairs
$(\mathbf{u}_i,\mathbf{v}_j),\,j\neq i$ apart,
$$
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{InfoNCE}}
=-\frac1B\sum_{i=1}^{B}
\log\frac{\exp\!\big(\langle\mathbf{u}_i,\mathbf{v}_i\rangle/\tau\big)}
{\sum_{j=1}^{B}\exp\!\big(\langle\mathbf{u}_i,\mathbf{v}_j\rangle/\tau\big)} .
$$ {#eq-ch09-infonce}
This is not a heuristic: at its optimum InfoNCE bounds the mutual information
between the paired views from below,
$I(\mathbf{u};\mathbf{v})\ge\log B-\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{InfoNCE}}$, so minimizing
the loss raises a lower bound on the shared information, and a larger batch (more
negatives) tightens the bound [@vandenoord2018representation]. The bound holds
because $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{InfoNCE}}$ is the cross-entropy of classifying the
positive among $B$ candidates; its infimum is $\log B-I(\mathbf{u};\mathbf{v})$,
attained when the implicit critic equals the density ratio
$p(\mathbf{v}\mid\mathbf{u})/p(\mathbf{v})$, so the loss can never fall below
that value. This makes the "align the modalities" intuition precise: alignment is
the maximization of an estimator of $I(\mathbf{u};\mathbf{v})$.

The template for the symmetric version is CLIP [@radford2021learning], which
aligns an image encoder and a text encoder by averaging the two retrieval
directions. With unit-normalized embeddings
$\hat{\mathbf{u}}_i=\mathbf{u}_i/\lVert\mathbf{u}_i\rVert$,
$\hat{\mathbf{v}}_j=\mathbf{v}_j/\lVert\mathbf{v}_j\rVert$, and similarity matrix
$S_{ij}=\langle\hat{\mathbf{u}}_i,\hat{\mathbf{v}}_j\rangle$, its loss is the mean
of a modality-2-retrieval cross-entropy and its transpose,
$$
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CLIP}}
=\frac12\Bigg(
-\frac1B\sum_{i=1}^{B}\log\frac{e^{S_{ii}/\tau}}{\sum_{j=1}^{B}e^{S_{ij}/\tau}}
-\frac1B\sum_{i=1}^{B}\log\frac{e^{S_{ii}/\tau}}{\sum_{j=1}^{B}e^{S_{ji}/\tau}}
\Bigg).
$$ {#eq-ch09-clip}
Minimizing @eq-ch09-clip over the two encoders drives the similarity matrix
toward the identity on each paired batch; the two terms are the
$\mathbf{u}\!\to\!\mathbf{v}$ and $\mathbf{v}\!\to\!\mathbf{u}$ retrieval
objectives, so a match missed in *either* direction is penalized.

Alignment is not free. By @eq-ch09-dpi the shared component recoverable from
a cross-modal objective is capped by $I(\mathbf{x}^{(1)};\mathbf{x}^{(2)})$, and
neither @eq-ch09-infonce nor @eq-ch09-clip contains a term that rewards
retaining the private term $H(\mathbf{x}^{(1)}\mid\mathbf{x}^{(2)})$; an encoder
can therefore satisfy the contrastive loss while discarding modality-specific
variation entirely. This is why contrastive alignment is paired with a
reconstruction or private-latent term when modality-specific signal matters
[@gong2021cobolt].

Applied to biology, this objective needs *paired* data — the same cell measured
in two modalities. CITE-seq provides exactly that pairing for RNA and protein;
chromatin and transcriptome pairs come from multiome assays. Contrastive
alignment is attractive because it yields embeddings usable for cross-modal
retrieval ("find the proteins matching this RNA profile") and because it does not
assume a shared decoder. Its weaknesses are the need for large paired batches and
the sensitivity of the learned space to how negatives are sampled. In biological
data the "negatives" are not random: two cells of the same type are near-duplicates,
and treating them as negatives teaches the model to separate cells that should be
close. Effective implementations therefore use in-batch or hard-negative mining
that respects cell-type structure, and they must be evaluated on held-out
modality pairs rather than on the same batch used for training. For
sequence–structure alignment, the same idea underlies models that embed a
protein sequence and its structure in a comparable space, using structure
predictors such as AlphaFold [@jumper2021highly] or inverse-folding models
[@hsu2022learning].

# Translation Between Modalities

Alignment asks whether two modalities can be compared; **translation** asks
whether one can be predicted from the other. Spatial transcriptomics is the
canonical case in this chapter: given a tissue image and a dissociated scRNA-seq
reference, predict the spatial location of each cell type. Tangram
[@biancalani2021deep] learns a nonnegative soft-assignment matrix
$T\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}^{\,n_{\mathrm{ref}}\times n_{\mathrm{sp}}}$ mapping
$n_{\mathrm{ref}}$ reference cells onto $n_{\mathrm{sp}}$ spatial spots. Writing
$\mathbf{Y}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{\mathrm{sp}}\times g}$ for the observed spot
expression and
$\mathbf{X}_{\mathrm{ref}}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{\mathrm{ref}}\times g}$ for the
dissociated reference, it maximizes expression concordance subject to a mapping
regularizer,
$$
\max_{T\ge0}\;
\sum_{k=1}^{n_{\mathrm{sp}}}
\cos\!\Big(\big(T^{\top}\mathbf{X}_{\mathrm{ref}}\big)_{k},\,\mathbf{Y}_{k}\Big)
\;-\;\lambda\,\Omega(T),
$$ {#eq-ch09-translation}
where, in @eq-ch09-translation,
$\big(T^{\top}\mathbf{X}_{\mathrm{ref}}\big)_{k}$ is the predicted expression of
spot $k$, $\cos(\cdot,\cdot)$ is the cosine similarity of Appendix A, $\Omega(T)$
penalizes degenerate mappings (for example, many reference cells collapsing onto
one spot), and $\lambda\ge0$ trades concordance against the regularizer. The
learned rows of $T$ are the cross-modal interface: each spot is represented as a
mixture of the reference cells assigned to it. SpaGCN
[@hu2021spagcn] instead embeds each spot
in histology-space, combining gene expression with image features and spatial
coordinates through a graph convolutional network to identify spatial domains.

Other translation directions follow the same pattern: sequence → structure
(AlphaFold [@jumper2021highly], and inverse folding for structure → sequence
[@hsu2022learning]), and RNA → protein or protein → RNA in CITE-seq via the joint
models above [@gayoso2021joint; @ashuach2023multivi]. In every case the embedding
is the interface: the two modalities are bridged because their representations
live in the same or comparable space.

# Missing Modalities and Partial Observability

Real multi-omic datasets are almost never complete. Some cells have only RNA,
some only ATAC, some both; spatial assays lose cells that dissociate; and donors
differ in which assays were run. Partial observability is a first-class modeling
requirement, not an edge case. Three strategies are common:

- **Marginal likelihood training.** Models such as MultiVI [@ashuach2023multivi]
  and totalVI [@gayoso2021joint] are trained so that a cell with only one
  modality present still contributes a valid likelihood term, yielding a latent
  embedding for every cell regardless of which views were measured.
- **Factor models with missing-view priors.** MOFA+ [@argelaguet2020mofa]
  handles missing modalities within its Bayesian inference by integrating over
  unobserved views.
- **Alignment plus imputation.** Contrastive models can impute a missing
  modality by nearest-neighbor retrieval in the aligned space, at the cost of
  treating a prediction as an observation — a step that must be reported
  explicitly because it can bias downstream analysis.

The design principle is that missingness should be part of the generative
process, so that a cell's embedding depends on *which* modalities were observed
rather than pretending all views exist. This has an evaluation consequence:
integration methods must be compared under the same pattern of missingness,
because a method that looks strong on fully paired data can degrade sharply when
only one modality is observed, and vice versa. Reporting the observed-modality
pattern alongside the integration score is therefore as important as reporting
the score itself.

# Case Study: Spatial Transcriptomics Embeddings

Spatial transcriptomics makes the integration problem concrete. Each spot carries
(i) a gene-expression count vector, (ii) two spatial coordinates, and usually
(iii) a histology image patch. The task is to place cell types and gene programs
in space, which requires aligning a dissociated reference (high resolution, no
space) with the spatial assay (space, lower resolution).

Tangram [@biancalani2021deep] learns a mapping from reference cells to spatial
voxels by optimizing expression similarity with a regularizer that discourages
mapping many cells to one spot; the resulting alignment supports both cell-type
placement and "spatial" gene expression. SpaGCN [@hu2021spagcn] builds a graph
whose nodes are spots and whose edges encode spatial proximity, expression
similarity, and image similarity, then applies graph convolution to smooth the
embedding and detect spatial domains. Both treat the embedding as the shared
medium across expression, image, and coordinates — the same shared-latent-space
logic as the non-spatial models, with space as an additional modality.

```python
import muon as mu
mdata = mu.read_h5mu("rna_atac.h5mu")
mu.pp.intersect_obs(mdata)
mu.tl.mofa(mdata, n_factors=15)      # shared factors across modalities
mu.tl.neighbors(mdata, n_neighbors=15)
```

The practical lesson from the case study generalizes: choose the fusion point
according to what the downstream task needs. If the goal is a joint embedding of
cells measured in different assays, intermediate fusion with missing-modality
training is the robust default; if the goal is cross-modal retrieval, contrastive
alignment is the natural fit; if the goal is a compact interpretable summary of
shared variation, factor analysis remains competitive.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Key Takeaways
- Multimodal integration decomposes variation into shared and modality-specific
  factors; a good embedding preserves both rather than discarding private signal
  to force alignment.
- Fusion happens early (concatenate), late (combine predictions), or
  intermediate (shared latent space); intermediate fusion is what enables
  cross-modal transfer and missing-view handling.
- MOFA+ [@argelaguet2020mofa] gives interpretable, linear shared factors;
  MultiVI [@ashuach2023multivi] and Cobolt [@gong2021cobolt] give nonlinear
  shared latents and support partially observed cells; WNN
  [@hao2021integrated] fuses per-modality graphs.
- Contrastive objectives in the CLIP/InfoNCE family [@radford2021learning;
  @vandenoord2018representation] align paired modalities without a shared
  decoder, and power cross-modal retrieval and sequence–structure alignment.
- Translation (spatial placement, modality imputation, structure prediction)
  relies on the shared space as the interface; spatial transcriptomics
  [@biancalani2021deep; @hu2021spagcn] is the clearest worked example.
- Missing modalities must be handled inside the model, not imputed silently; a
  cell's embedding should depend on which views were actually observed.
:::
